To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the performance of cryptographic protocols on current smart-cards and Android smart-phones is still too poor for the implementation of advanced cryptographic protocols.

(i) the current smart-card technology is not suitable for the implementation of privacy-enhancing protocols, (ii) the current Android smart-phones are not suitable for the secure implementation of privacy-enhancement protocols, (iii) the current tablet technology (Android and Windows) is suitable for the secure and efficient implementation of privacy-enhancements protocols, but the implementation of such protocols is not suitable for current smart-phones.

(1) the performance of cryptographic protocols can be estimated using our tool; (2) the performance of smart-cards is significantly worse than that of smart-phones; (3) the smart-phone performance is not significantly worse than that predicted by the tool; (4) the tool is not accurate enough to predict the smart-card performance; (5) the smart-card performance is significantly worse than the tool estimates.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the cryptographic constructions used in the privacy-enhancing schemes can be practically implemented in a user-friendly and cost-effective manner.
the question whether the current state of the art in privacy-enhancing cryptography is suitable for the implementation on current smart-cards and smartphones.
the question of how to make privacy-enhancing schemes more usable in real-life applications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cryptographic primitives are not only feasible on smart-cards, but they also provide a reasonable performance.
the performance of smart-cards has not been significantly improved in the last decade.
current smart-cards are not capable to provide a reasonable performance for privacy-preserving protocols and thus cannot be used in practical applications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

all major smart-card and smart-phone platforms are able to execute cryptographic protocols which are based on the fundamental cryptographic primitives, such as elliptic-curve scalar multiplication and exponentiation, efficiently.
the current state of the smart-card and smart-phone technology does not support the implementation of the cryptographic constructions used in advanced cryptographic schemes.
the cryptographic primitives are fast enough to be used in privacy-enhanced protocols.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the current generation of smart-cards and Android-based smart-phones can be used to efficiently implement the fundamental cryptographic primitives used in privacy-enhancement schemes.
smart-cards and Android devices can provide sufficient performance for the practical use of privacy-enhancing cryptography in the near future.

the current state-of-the-art privacy-enhancing schemes can not be implemented on contemporary smart-cars and smart-phones, and that the performance of the cryptographic primitives is not the main obstacle.
